blocks.text: 6. Practicing Chan and Pure Land Together

inline.s: A Chan practitioner came to visit and asked: "At the moment of death, if one has not yet seen one's nature (fully perceived the inherent nature), or has seen one's nature but not yet severed the delusion of thought, what plan can put an end to birth-and-death?"

[Delusion of view and delusion of thought] The delusion of view and the delusion of thought. The delusion of view is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in matters of view, such as the five false views of self-view, extremist view, perverted view, view-attachment, and precept-attachment; the delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in matters of thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and endure birth-and-death in vain; severing them enables one to end birth-and-death and escape the three realms.
Answer: Practice Chan and Pure Land together.
Question: Why practice Chan and Pure Land together?

Answer: Mazu established the monastery (the Chan temple), and Baizhang laid down the pure rules (the "essential rules of the monastery"). These pure rules were established for the Chan practitioners in the monastery, and they say at the outset:
"A monastery flourishes by having no affairs; in practice, Buddha-recitation is the most certain."

The second sentence, "in practice, Buddha-recitation is the most certain," means that for the sake of certainty, a Chan practitioner, while investigating Chan, should also believe, vow, and recite the Buddha's name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land (practicing Chan and Pure Land together). This is because, by reciting the Buddha's name and being reborn in the Western Pure Land, one ends birth-and-death merely by subduing affliction; whereas one who investigates Chan, in order to end birth-and-death, must sever the delusions of view and thought. In comparison the former is far easier, and so is the more certain path. Many patriarchs and great masters practiced Chan and Pure Land together, making the Pure Land their final return. For example, Master Yongming Yanshou, Master Hanshan, Master Chewu, and others. National Master Puzhao, the author of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, also practiced the two together and wrote the Essential Gate of Buddha-Recitation. Master Yongming Yanshou composed the Four Selections, advocating the joint practice of Chan and the Pure Land. His verse reads:
With Chan but without the Pure Land, nine of ten men miss the way; when the shadow of the karmic state appears, in a flash he goes along with it.
Without Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitabha, how can one worry not to awaken?
With Chan and with the Pure Land, he is like a tiger wearing horns: a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch.
Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar await; through myriad kalpas and a thousand births, there is no one to rely upon.

[Selection] Distinguishing and choosing among meanings. [The Four Selections] Four judgments of selection. [With Chan] Seeing one's nature (fully perceiving the inherent nature). [With the Pure Land] True faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha's name with single-minded focus. [Without Chan] Not having seen one's nature. [Without the Pure Land] Not having accomplished "true faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha's name with single-minded focus."
Question: As long as one has faith and vow and holds the name, it is "having the Pure Land." Why require that one's Buddha-recitation reach single-minded focus?

Answer: Master Ouyi (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school), in his Essentials of the Amitabha Sutra, expressly teaches: without the wondrous practice of single-minded Buddha-recitation, one cannot prove his true faith or fulfill his earnest vow. (The original says:
"Practice is to hold fast the name, with single-minded focus." "Without the wondrous practice of upholding the Name, one cannot fulfill one's vow and prove one's faith."
Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) says:
"Single-minded focus is the final destination of the pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, then it is never certain."

(From the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu.) If one's Buddha-recitation has not yet reached single-minded focus, how can it be called "having the Pure Land," and "of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go"?
Now I shall explain the Four Selections as follows:
[With Chan but without the Pure Land, nine of ten men miss the way; when the shadow of the karmic state appears, in a flash he goes along with it.]

If one investigates Chan and sees one's nature but has not severed the delusions of view and thought (this is true of nine out of ten among those who have awakened), then when the shadow of the karmic state appears at death, he immediately follows the karmic force to be reborn, quite unable to be his own master. Yet because the awakening has already severed the delusion of view, he will not be born again in an evil realm.

[Nine of ten men miss the way] Among those who have seen their nature, at least nine-tenths have not severed the delusions of view and thought. For them, to practice Chan alone is a mistaken path, because they cannot leave the round of rebirth. [Miss chuo] Error, mistake. [Shadow of the karmic state] The state of the intermediate body, that is, the manifestation at the moment of death of the karmic forces of good and evil from this life and all past lives. The instant this state appears, in the blink of an eye one goes to be reborn in a good or evil realm following the most violent of those karmic forces, without the slightest mastery over oneself. [In a flash] Suddenly, rapidly.
[Without Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitabha, how can one worry not to awaken?]

Although one has not yet seen one's nature, with true faith and earnest vow and single-minded Buddha-recitation one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land with absolute certainty (of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go). Having gone to the Western Pure Land and seen Amitabha Buddha, one accomplishes Buddhahood in a single lifetime. How could one still worry about not seeing one's nature?
[With Chan and with the Pure Land, he is like a tiger wearing horns: a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch.]

Having already seen one's nature, and with true faith and earnest vow and single-minded Buddha-recitation, one is a teacher of men in this life. At the moment of death he is reborn in the highest grade in the Western Pure Land, accomplishing Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Single-minded Buddha-recitation has the single-minded focus of affairs and the single-minded focus of principle. For one who has seen his nature (who has Chan) to recite the Buddha's name is the single-minded focus of principle; having gone to the Western Pure Land he is reborn in the highest grade, and to be a teacher and a Buddha is entirely natural. As for the single-minded focus of affairs and the single-minded focus of principle, see our academy's textbook
Detailed Explanation of the Record of Feeling the Samadhi of Buddha-Recollection
[Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar await; through myriad kalpas and a thousand births, there is no one to rely upon.]

If one has not seen his nature and has not accomplished "true faith and earnest vow, single-minded Buddha-recitation," then if at death he cannot keep his right mindfulness clear, he is drawn by karmic force and reborn among the six realms. Because he has not severed the delusion of view, he will revolve through the evil realms, and the time spent in hell (the iron bed and the bronze pillar) is the longest. The Buddha says: "Those who gain a human body are like the soil on a fingernail; those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth."
Question: To practice Chan and at the same time believe, vow, and recite the Buddha's name, is this not mixing things up, standing with one foot in each of two boats?

Answer: It is not standing in two boats, but boarding the one boat by which one can reach the other shore in this very life. The aim of our study of Buddhism is to become a Buddha and to deliver sentient beings. To become a Buddha, one must first put an end to birth-and-death by division and escape the round of rebirth, and then end birth-and-death by transformation and realize the Buddha-fruit. For this one life, the urgent task is to end birth-and-death by division and escape the round of rebirth. Those who can sever the delusions of view and thought lie outside the scope of our discussion. For those who cannot sever these two delusions, there are three boats: cultivating the Pure Land, cultivating Chan, and cultivating Chan and the Pure Land together. Cultivating the Pure Land is the business of students of the Pure Land school; we discuss only the two boats of cultivating Chan and of cultivating the two together.

If one cultivates Chan alone, there are two outcomes: having Chan without the Pure Land, and having neither Chan nor the Pure Land. Neither can end birth-and-death and escape the round of rebirth. In particular, to cultivate Chan yet not see one's nature has extremely grave consequences: the iron bed and the bronze pillar. Therefore, to end birth-and-death and escape the round of rebirth there is only one boat: to practice Chan and the Pure Land together. As for whether this joint practice is a mixing, so long as one uses it well, it is not only unmixed but mutually enhancing; you will soon know this for yourself. Think about it: if it were a mixing, why would Patriarch Yongming say "with Chan and with the Pure Land, he is like a tiger wearing horns: a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch"? Patriarch Yongming himself was a man who had come through the joint practice, and in his own practice he personally proved that the two together enhance each other, "like a tiger wearing horns, a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch."

[Birth-and-death by division] Sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because they are recompensed by good and evil karma, have a fixed limit to their lifespan and a distinct division to their bodies; therefore their birth-and-death is called "birth-and-death by division." One who ends birth-and-death by division is freed of the round of rebirth and has escaped the three realms. [Birth-and-death by transformation] The sages of the three vehicles, having severed the delusions of view and thought and ended birth-and-death by division, in the course of cultivation have deluded thoughts gradually extinguished and realization gradually increased; this shifting of delusion and awakening differs in each period, and the passage from a former period to a later one is, as it were, a dying and a becoming, whose change is subtle, mysterious, and inconceivable. Hence it is called "birth-and-death by transformation." One who ends birth-and-death by transformation fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.
Question: Then why cultivate Chan?
Answer: Cultivating Chan is suited to the following circumstances:
First, those who in this life can sever the delusions of view and thought, or even those who seek to transcend the Dharma-body, should cultivate Chan.
Second, the distinctive character of Chinese Buddhism lies in Chan. Those who wish to thoroughly understand Chinese Buddhism and revive Chinese Buddhism should cultivate Chan.
Third, those who wish to be a horned tiger and widely deliver sentient beings should cultivate Chan.

Fourth, in terms of practice, the Chan school has a vast and profound body of theory, methods, and cases, perfect and sudden, keen and swift. Those whose faculties accord with Chan and who delight in it should cultivate Chan.
Question: How does one practice Chan and Pure Land together?

Answer: Investigating Chan in order to see one's nature has three stages: first, the coarse thought subsides (ten thousand thoughts converge into one); second, the fine thought subsides (the one returns to nothingness); third, the subtlest thought comes to rest and one fully perceives the inherent nature. Having, by investigating Chan, brought ten thousand thoughts to converge into one, or the one to return to nothingness, or even seen one's nature, a practitioner's Buddha-recitation can reach single-minded focus. But to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, besides single-minded Buddha-recitation, one must also have true faith and an earnest vow. Trust means steadfastly trusting in the Buddha's power. When Amitabha Buddha was on the causal ground he made forty-eight vows, each one to deliver sentient beings; and the Buddha's compassionate power gathers in sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If, at the moment of death, I concentrate my right mindfulness within, like a child remembering his mother, I can surely move the Buddha to come and welcome me. Vow means being willing to be reborn in this very lifetime in the Western Pure Land, no longer sinking and rising for many lives and many kalpas in this defiled place, going from delusion into delusion. And having vowed to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, one vows to return to the Saha world to deliver all sentient beings. Therefore, in the joint practice of Chan and the Pure Land, one must solidly and genuinely exert effort in true faith and earnest vow, and attain single-minded Buddha-recitation, so that at death one earnestly seeks rebirth in the Western Pure Land, concentrating right mindfulness within and drawing the Buddha's welcome from without. As for true faith, earnest vow, and the method of Buddha-recitation, see our academy's textbook
Aware Buddha-Recitation

[Coarse thought, fine thought, and subtlest thought] For example, for one who is reciting the Buddha's name, wandering thoughts are the coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is the fine thought. Usually, when both the coarse and the fine thoughts have subsided, this is called no-thought, which is the no-thought ordinarily meant. Beyond this, if the subtlest thought also comes to rest, this is the ultimate no-thought. [Subtlest thought] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing of the cognitive mind is the characteristic mark of the alaya consciousness.
Question: What are the differences and the similarities between Chan and the Pure Land?

Answer: In terms of practice, whichever gate one takes, the path is all the same: ten thousand thoughts converge into one, the one returns to nothingness, one sees one's nature, severs the delusions of view and thought, attains the patience with the unborn, and fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.

The Pure Land school is to recite Amitabha Buddha of the Western Pure Land and to seek rebirth there. As long as through Buddha-recitation one reaches the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one (single-minded focus), at death one is certainly reborn in the Western Pure Land. When the flower opens and one sees the Buddha, one at once attains the patience with the unborn, and then fully realizes the Buddha-fruit. If, having attained single-minded focus, one wishes to raise the grade of rebirth, one may further cultivate the samadhi of Buddha-recitation so that the one returns to nothingness and one sees one's nature (as for the samadhi of Buddha-recitation, see our academy's textbook
Detailed Explanation of the Record of Feeling the Samadhi of Buddha-Recollection
. Of course, one may also continue further, severing the delusions of view and thought and then attaining the patience with the unborn.

Investigating Chan, by raising the topic of meditation, brings ten thousand thoughts into one, then the one returns to nothingness, then one sees one's nature; afterward one severs the delusions of view and thought; then one attains the patience with the unborn.

Contemplating the mind, by observing the flowing consciousness of the karma presently manifesting in one's own mind, brings ten thousand thoughts into one, then the one returns to nothingness, then one sees one's nature; afterward one severs the delusions of view and thought; then one attains the patience with the unborn.

The Pure Land school, with faith, vow, and the upholding of the Name, needs only to reach the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one (single-minded focus) in order to end birth-and-death. The two great gates of the Chan school, investigating Chan and contemplating the mind, both require one to sever the delusions of view and thought before one can end birth-and-death.
Question: The fourth patriarch of the Chan school, Master Daoxin, says:

"The objects and conditions of the world are neither good nor bad; good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, whence can false emotion arise? Since false emotion does not arise, the true mind is free to know all things. Only let the mind be at ease according to itself, with no more opposing treatment; this is called the everlasting Dharma-body, without any change."
This instruction is the most direct method of practice. Why must one "converge ten thousand thoughts into one, return the one to nothingness, see one's nature, and so on"?

Answer: This instruction of the fourth patriarch was given to Master Farong of Mount Niutou (see the Record of the Five Lamps). At that time Farong had already cultivated to the point of "the marvel of a hundred birds bringing flowers," and "the fourth patriarch, observing the atmosphere from afar, knew that there was an extraordinary person on that mountain (Mount Niutou), and so went in person to seek him out." Therefore the fourth patriarch gave him, in a pointed way, the gate of spontaneous operation: "Only let the mind be at ease according to itself, with no more opposing treatment." But for ordinary people, if when confronted with circumstances they cannot manage not to "forcibly name" them, then they should first enter the gate of opposing treatment and begin with the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one and so forth. In fact, before Farong met the fourth patriarch, he too had begun with the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one and so forth, or else in a former life he had begun there. This principle is thoroughly set forth in the Essentials of Mind Cultivation;
